title: Network Delay Time
statement:
A CDN pushes a config update from one origin server to every edge server. There are n servers, numbered 1 to n. Each entry [u, v, w] in times is a one-way link: an update that reaches server u reaches server v w milliseconds later. Every server forwards the update on all its outgoing links as soon as it gets it.

Write def solution(times, n, k). The update starts at server k at time 0. Return the time, in milliseconds, at which the last server receives it. That is the largest shortest-path distance from k. If some server can never receive it, return -1.

examples.why: The LeetCode 743 example 1. Servers 1 and 3 get it at 1, server 4 at 2.
The LeetCode 743 example 2. One link of 1 ms.
The LeetCode 743 example 3. The only link goes from 1 to 2, so server 1 never receives the update.

constraints: 1 ≤ u, v ≤ n and u ≠ v
two links may join the same pair of servers with different delays

think.q: When does one server receive the update, and what do you return?
think.a: A server receives the update at the length of its shortest path from k, where a path's length is the sum of its link delays. The answer is the maximum of those shortest distances over all n servers, or -1 if one is unreachable. Links are one-way, and server k itself has time 0.

Server 1 at 0. Server 3 at 2 (direct). Server 2: direct is 9, but via 3 it is 2 + 3 = 5. So server 2 gets it at 5, and the last arrival is 5. The direct link is not always the fastest; the fewest hops is not always the fastest either.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Bellman-Ford: start every distance at infinity except k (0), then go over every link and lower dist[v] to dist[u] + w when that is smaller. Repeat until a full pass changes nothing; at most n - 1 passes are needed. That is O(n x E), which is slow when a long chain is listed backwards.

Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap. All delays are non-negative, so the server with the smallest tentative time can be finalised: no later path can beat it. Pop it from a heapq, relax its outgoing links, and push any improved neighbours. BFS is not enough, because links have different delays.

1. Build an adjacency list graph[u] = [(v, w), ...].
  2. dist = {} for finished servers; heap = [(0, k)].
  3. Pop (d, u). If u is already finished, skip it (it is a stale entry). Otherwise set dist[u] = d and push (d + w, v) for every unfinished neighbour.
  4. When the heap is empty: if len(dist) < n return -1, else return max(dist.values()).

One server (answer 0). A server with no incoming link (-1). Links that point only away from k's part of the graph. A longer path that is faster than a direct link. Two links between the same pair. Zero-delay links. A long chain listed backwards, which makes Bellman-Ford do one pass per link.

hints: Each server receives the update along its fastest path. The answer is the slowest of those fastest arrivals.
Delays differ, so BFS by hop count is wrong. Which algorithm finds shortest paths when every edge weight is non-negative?
Use heapq with (time, server) pairs. When you pop a server for the first time, its time is final; skip it if you pop it again.
explain:
Example 4, times = [[1, 2, 9], [1, 3, 2], [3, 2, 3], [2, 4, 1], [3, 4, 10]], n = 4, k = 1:

  • Heap [(0, 1)]. Pop server 1: final time 0. Push (9, 2) and (2, 3).
  • Pop (2, 3): final 2. Push (5, 2) and (12, 4).
  • Pop (5, 2): final 5. Push (6, 4).
  • Pop (6, 4): final 6. Pop (9, 2) and (12, 4): both stale, skipped.

All 4 servers are final with times 0, 5, 2, 6. Return 6. The key fact: because no delay is negative, the smallest time in the heap cannot be improved by any path through a server with a larger time. So the first pop of each server is its true arrival time, and the stale entries are just skipped.
complexity: O(E log E) time with the heap, O(n + E) space
